newsitem.title: USA: NASA seeks to patch-up tattered telescope.
newsitem.headline: NASA seeks to patch-up tattered telescope.

text.p: NASA engineers sought ways to patch up the Hubble Space Telescope's torn and tattered exterior on Sunday as Discovery's astronauts completed another day's work on the orbiting observatory.
Mark Lee and Steve Smith, making the third spacewalk of the mission, took a close up look at some of the tears and cracks in the foil skin of the telescope.

"Basically this thing is just falling apart, cracking all over the place," Lee told mission control, as he inspected a foil-covered door on the telescope. The tattered material did not appear to be brittle, he added.
Lee tried taping up a crack, but as NASA engineers had suspected, the adhesive failed to work.
"It barely sticks," he said. "It doesn't do anything."
NASA officials were worried that the torn material could peel off and contaminate the telescope's delicate optics.

"The damage to the ... blankets on (Hubble) has many folks concerned," mission control wrote to the shuttle crew on Saturday in a electronic message. "We are currently investigating potential repair options but concede that it will be a difficult task."
Lee and Smith collected pieces of spare foil, tape and cords for a possible repair during the mission's fourth and final spacewalk, scheduled for Sunday night.

Engineers suspected that variations in temperature and ultraviolet rays from the sun had caused the silvery foil to crack and tear. The damage, which appeared extensive, was not seen when astronauts last visited the telescope in 1993.

Lee and Smith completed upgraded three more components of the telescope during their seven-hour spacewalk. They completed what was considered the most challenging task of the effort, the replacement of a faulty electronics box.

The replacement of the data interface unit, which relays computer commands to various telescope components, was difficult because the device was not designed to be handled by astronauts wearing bulky space suit gloves.
Working in a jumble of wires, Lee had to make 18 cable connections to complete the installation.
"Great hands, Mark," mission control's Jeff Hoffman radioed once the work was done.
The two men then went on to exchange an ageing reel-to-reel tape recorder for a new digital model and replace a broken flywheel, used to manoeuvre the telescope.
"You guys are batting 100 percent," radioed mission control's Marc Garneau as the two men completed their work.
Between tasks, the astronauts marvelled at the spectacular view as the shuttle soared more than 370 miles (595 km) above the Pacific, off the west coast of Australia.
"Holy cow!" Lee exclaimed. "I've got the Hubble Space Telescope, Shark's Bay, and the planet earth and the moon in my view. What a great place to be."
"Just an average day for a couple of spacewalkers," Joe Tanner remarked from inside the shuttle's cabin.

As the astronauts ended their spacewalk, shuttle commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz fired the shuttle's smallest manoeuvring jets for 20 minutes to nudge the Hubble into a higher orbit.
NASA hopes to boost the telescope's altitude by a total of 5 miles (8 km) to prolong its lifetime.
